title: Your Brain Edits What You See
principle: What you see is not a picture of the world.

t: There is a hole in your vision, in both eyes, right now. You have never noticed it.
Each of your eyes has a patch with no light detectors at all — where the nerve leaves. You have a blind spot in your field of view at this moment, and you cannot find it by looking.
sub: You do not see a gap. That is the part that needs explaining.

question: Why do you not see a black hole where the blind spot is?
Why is the blind spot not perceived as a gap?
options: Your brain fills it in with a guess from around it
The hole is too small to notice
stages.outcome: Your brain fills it in with a guess from around it
note: Guess first, then go and check it on yourself.
Commit. The next stage has you demonstrate this on your own eye, so your answer is about to be tested.

stages.label: Try it on yourself
captions: Hold up your left thumb and your right thumb, about 20 cm apart, at arm's length.
Close your LEFT eye. With your right eye, stare hard at your left thumb. Do not let your gaze move.
Still staring at the left thumb, slowly move your right thumb further to the right.
Keep staring. At some point your right thumb vanishes completely — and comes back if you move further.
It did not go dark where it vanished. You saw background there instead.
t: You can find your own blind spot right now. Follow each step.
This works on you, today, with no equipment. Follow the steps and keep your gaze fixed — the effect disappears the moment your eye moves.
after: Your thumb disappeared and nothing black appeared. Your brain made something up.
The thumb vanished and was replaced by plausible background rather than by darkness. Nothing reported the absence, because the filling-in happens before anything you can introspect on.

t: What you see is not a picture of the world. It is your brain's best guess.
Perception is not reception. Your brain builds a model from incomplete data and you experience the model, not the data.
Perception is inference. The retinal image is ambiguous, low-resolution outside the fovea, interrupted by the optic disc and smeared by eye movement — and none of that reaches awareness.

Helmholtz called it unconscious inference in the 1860s and the framing has held up. The visual system is solving an underdetermined problem — infinitely many scenes are consistent with any retinal image — and it resolves it using assumptions about the world. Those assumptions are usually right, which is why illusions are interesting: they are the cases where a normally-correct assumption is wrong.
sub: Most of the time the guess is right, so you never notice you are guessing.
The guess is usually correct, which is exactly why it is invisible. You only catch it when it fails.
You are also blind for about 40 minutes a day during saccades, and never experience a single moment of it.

Your eyes make several rapid movements a second and vision is suppressed during each one. Add it up and it is a substantial fraction of waking life spent not seeing, edited out so smoothly that the edit itself is undetectable from the inside.

q: Is what you see the same as what is there?
What is the relationship between the retinal image and what you perceive?
In what sense is perception inferential rather than receptive?
options: No — it is your brain's best guess from what arrives
Yes, your eyes send a picture to your brain
Yes, unless you have something wrong with your eyes
why: Your eyes do not send a picture. They send patches of information with holes in it, and your brain builds something complete out of that. You just showed yourself one of the holes.

The image is incomplete, and what you experience is a reconstruction. You demonstrated the point yourself: the thumb vanished and background appeared, which means something manufactured that background.

The mapping from scene to retinal image loses information irreversibly, so recovering the scene is underdetermined and requires assumptions. Perception is the output of that inference. Illusions are not malfunctions — they are the inference machinery running correctly on input it was not built for.

t: It is why eyewitnesses can be completely honest and completely wrong.

An eyewitness is not replaying a recording; they are reporting a reconstruction, built from incomplete input and filled in with what was probable. Confidence does not track accuracy, because the filling-in is invisible from the inside — a witness cannot feel the difference between what they saw and what their brain supplied. This is now well enough established that many courts instruct juries about it.
